--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Introduction to Project Management and Communication ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: 1. **Distinguish** a project from a process, and explain why project work needs its own discipline. 2. **Describe** the triple constraint (scope, time, cost) and its relationship to quality and resources. 3. **Identify** the five process phases of a project and what happens in each. 4. **Apply** the project manager's decision hierarchy and name the four pillars of the PMI Code of Ethics. 5. **Build** a project communication plan and choose the right method (formal/informal, written/verbal) for a message. 6. **Calculate** the number of communication channels on a team and explain why they grow faster than headcount. 7. **Apply** active- and effective-listening techniques and recognize the listening filters that distort a message. 8. **Select** the appropriate performance report (status, progress, trend, forecast, variance, earned value) for a stakeholder need.
Before we begin: think of a group assignment that went badly Was the problem that nobody knew *what* to do, or that people knew but never told each other? Most project failures are communication failures wearing a different coat. Keep that example in mind.
## Introduction: only one project in four Here is a sobering number that opens this course: by common industry estimates, only about **26 % of projects** are delivered successfully while respecting the triple constraint --- on scope, on time, on budget. The other three in four slip, overspend, descope, or fail outright. That is why project management exists as a discipline. Running the RC-vehicle launch from the last chapter is not the same as running a production line. A line is a **process**: repetitive, permanent, tuned once and then kept stable. A **project** is a one-time push toward a unique goal, under a deadline and a budget, and it needs different tools and a different mindset. ::: {.callout-important} **Case study --- Orion Tech (MGMT-3105, Week 2).** A software company built a healthcare app. The team was skilled, but: developers were never clear on requirements and reworked constantly; the PM ran everything through email and buried the team; stakeholders got no status reports; a few voices dominated meetings while others went silent; and tone and urgency were misread between the local team and offshore developers. Deadlines slipped, the budget grew, and the client's satisfaction collapsed. Leadership asked whether the PM had followed any communication protocol at all. :::
## Project versus process | | **Project** | **Process** | |---|---|---| | Duration | Temporary, one-time | Permanent, ongoing | | Work | Unique, complex, connected activities toward one goal | Repetitive, designed to be repeated | | Ends when | The goal is met (by a specific time, within budget, to spec) | It doesn't --- it is improved and kept running | | Example on our project | *Designing and launching the RC-vehicle replica* | *Moulding 100 000 bodies once the line is running* | Projects help companies cope with **shortened product life cycles**, **narrow launch windows**, **increasingly complex products**, and **global markets**. The RC-vehicle brief has all four: a holiday launch window, a technical product, and suppliers on two continents. ## The triple constraint Every project is boxed in by **scope**, **time**, and **cost**, with **quality** sitting in the middle as the measure of whether stakeholders are satisfied. Resources (people, equipment, facilities) are the fourth practical limit. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The triple constraint. Scope, time, and cost form the sides; quality is the area they enclose. Change one side and at least one other must move, or quality suffers.](02-Introduction-and-Communication_files/figure-html/fig-triple-constraint-02-1.png){#fig-triple-constraint-02 fig-align='center' width=768} ::: :::
Think about it: the retailer moves the RC-vehicle launch four weeks earlier. Which constraint gives? Time just shrank. To hold the launch you must either **cut scope** (fewer body options, defer a feature), **add cost** (overtime, expedited tooling, a second supplier), or **accept lower quality** (less testing) --- and that last one is how projects like Orion Tech's die. The PM's job is to make that trade explicit and get a decision, not to quietly absorb it.
### Try it yourself: put a number on each side of the triangle "Which constraint gives" is a much easier decision once each option has a dollar figure attached. Live cell --- change the weeks compressed, the costs, or the failure probability and see how the three options compare. ```{=html}

Triple-Constraint Trade-off Calculator

$ / wk
$
$
$
```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: triple-constraint-tradeoff-02 weeks_compressed <- 4 # Option A: hold scope -- pay to compress the schedule overtime_cost_per_week <- 9000 expedite_fee <- 15000 cost_of_holding_scope <- weeks_compressed * overtime_cost_per_week + expedite_fee # Option B: hold cost -- cut scope (drop one body colourway) colourway_revenue_at_risk <- 62000 # forecast contribution margin lost # Option C: hold cost and scope -- accept lower quality (skip one test cycle) skip_test_prob_failure <- 0.08 # chance a defect reaches the customer field_failure_cost <- 240000 # recall/rework cost if it does expected_quality_cost <- skip_test_prob_failure * field_failure_cost fmt <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE) costs <- c(A = cost_of_holding_scope, B = colourway_revenue_at_risk, C = expected_quality_cost) cheapest <- c(A = "A, pay to compress", B = "B, cut scope", C = "C, skip a test cycle")[[names(which.min(costs))]] par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) bp <- barplot(costs / 1000, names.arg = c("A: compress", "B: cut scope", "C: cut testing"), col = c("#2980b9", "#e67e22", "#8e44ad"), ylim = c(0, max(costs / 1000) * 1.2), ylab = "Cost of flexing ($ thousand)", main = "What each side of the triangle costs") text(bp, costs / 1000, labels = paste0("$", round(costs / 1000, 1), "k"), pos = 3, cex = 1.3) cat(sprintf("Cheapest side to flex: Option %s\n", cheapest)) cat(sprintf("Option A: pay to compress $%s\n", fmt(cost_of_holding_scope))) cat(sprintf("Option B: cut scope $%s revenue lost\n", fmt(colourway_revenue_at_risk))) cat(sprintf("Option C: skip a test cycle $%s expected cost\n", fmt(expected_quality_cost))) cat(sprintf("Option C risk %.0f%% chance of a $%s failure\n", skip_test_prob_failure * 100, fmt(field_failure_cost))) ```
## The five process phases ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Effort and resource use across the project life cycle. Little happens during initiation, effort peaks through execution and control, and it falls away at closing.](02-Introduction-and-Communication_files/figure-html/fig-project-lifecycle-02-1.png){#fig-project-lifecycle-02 fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: | Phase | Key work | |---|---| | **1. Initiating** | Business case, feasibility, project sponsors, **project charter** + sign-off. | | **2. Planning** | Scope statement, WBS, network diagram (AON), budget, risk plan, quality standards, control system, communication protocols. *This phase decides success or failure.* | | **3. Executing** | Execute the plan, monitor progress, quality assurance. The PM shifts from doing to leading. | | **4. Controlling** | Scope/change/schedule/budget/risk control become daily; overlaps execution. | | **5. Closing** | Final review of budget, schedule, scope; customer sign-off; **lessons learned**; release resources; final payments. The hardest phase to finish well. | ### The project manager's decision hierarchy When decisions conflict, this is the order of consideration: 1. **Safety** (always first) 2. What is best for **the company I represent** 3. What is best for **the project sponsor** 4. What is best for **the customer** 5. What is best for **the suppliers** And the **PMI Code of Ethics** rests on four pillars: **responsibility, respect, fairness, and honesty**. You can violate ethics without breaking a law --- but as an accredited PM you would swear to uphold the code, and breaking it puts your professional standing at risk. ## Project communications Communication is not a side task. **About 90 % of a project manager's time is spent communicating.** The three communication processes are **plan**, **manage**, and **control**. ### The communication plan A written communication plan is built from the stakeholders' information needs. Typical elements: - What information is collected, and when - Who receives it - How it is gathered and stored - Limits, if any, on who may tell whom - Reporting relationships - Contact information for all stakeholders - The distribution schedule for each type of communication
Orion Tech fix: what should have been in the plan on day one? A stakeholder list with each party's information needs; the report types (status, cost, risk, performance) and their frequency; the mix of channels (email for the record, chat for quick updates, dashboards for tracking, video for collaboration); and **feedback loops** so every team member confirms they understood the requirements. None of that existed --- so requirements were guessed at and stakeholders were left in the dark.
### The communication model Every communication has three elements: a **sender**, a **message**, and a **receiver**. The sender **encodes** the message based on the receiver's education, experience, language, and culture, picks the right method, and **confirms it was understood**. The receiver **decodes** carefully and checks their understanding. **Feedback** ("Does that make sense?", a nod, a clarifying question) closes the loop. ### Communication channels grow faster than the team Add one person to a team and you do not add one relationship --- you add one for every person already there. The number of two-way channels on a team of $n$ people is: $$\text{channels} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Two-way communication channels versus team size. Doubling the team roughly quadruples the channels that have to be kept coherent.](02-Introduction-and-Communication_files/figure-html/fig-channels-02-1.png){#fig-channels-02 fig-align='center' width=864} ::: ::: ### Worked Example 1: channels on the RC-vehicle project The core project has the PM, 4 team members, an accountant, and a sponsor liaison --- **7 people**. The extended stakeholder circle adds 2 supplier contacts, a retailer contact, and a compliance officer --- **11 people**. Live cell --- try different core-team and extended-circle sizes. ```{=html}

Communication Channels Calculator

```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: channels-example-02 core <- 7 extended <- 11 ch_core <- core * (core - 1) / 2 ch_extended <- extended * (extended - 1) / 2 n <- 2:40 par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) plot(n, n * (n - 1) / 2, type = "l", lwd = 4, col = "#2c3e50", xlab = "People in the group", ylab = "Communication channels", main = "Channels grow with the square of group size") points(c(core, extended), c(ch_core, ch_extended), pch = 19, cex = 2.2, col = c("#2980b9", "#e74c3c")) cat(sprintf("Widening the circle from %d to %d adds %d channels\n", core, extended, ch_extended - ch_core)) cat(sprintf("Core team channels %d\n", ch_core)) cat(sprintf("Extended circle channels %d\n", ch_extended)) ```
Four extra people did not add four conversations --- they added 34. That is the argument for a **hub-and-spoke** communication plan (routes defined, the PM as the hub) instead of letting everyone talk to everyone about everything. ### Try it yourself: channel growth and the cost of one more stakeholder ```{=html}

Cost of One More Stakeholder

```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: channels-calc-02 team_size <- 9 channels <- function(n) n * (n - 1) / 2 sizes <- team_size + 0:4 par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) plot(2:40, channels(2:40), type = "l", lwd = 4, col = "#bdc3c7", xlab = "People in the group", ylab = "Communication channels", main = "Each added person costs more than the last") points(sizes, channels(sizes), pch = 19, cex = 2.2, col = c("#2980b9", rep("#e74c3c", 4))) cat(sprintf("Adding person #%d alone creates %d new channels\n", team_size + 1, channels(team_size + 1) - channels(team_size))) for (extra in 0:4) { n <- team_size + extra cat(sprintf("Team of %d %d channels", n, channels(n))) if (extra > 0) cat(sprintf(" (+%d vs. baseline)", channels(n) - channels(team_size))) cat("\n") } ```
## Listening: the mode we use most and understand least The four modes of communication, by share of a typical day and by how well they are scientifically understood: | Mode | Share | Notes | |---|---:|---| | Listening | ~55 % | The most used, the **least** studied and taught | | Speaking | ~23 % | | | Reading | ~13 % | | | Writing | ~9 % | | And most of the meaning is **nonverbal**: roughly **93 %** of person-to-person communication is carried by body language (~55 %) and tone of voice (~38 %) --- and tone's share rises toward 86 % on the phone, where body language is gone. - **Active listening:** the receiver signals engagement --- agreeing, asking for clarification. - **Effective listening:** watching the speaker for gesture and expression, thinking before responding, asking questions, repeating back, giving feedback. ### The listening filters Every message passes through three filters before it lands: - **Selective attention** --- we choose what to focus on. - **Selective interpretation** --- we impose our own meaning (shaped by gender, generation, geography, culture, education, occupation). - **Selective retention** --- we choose what to keep, and for how long. There is also a raw arithmetic problem. People **listen** at about 500 words per minute but **speak** at about 150. That leaves ~350 words per minute of spare capacity --- room to tune out. ### Try it yourself: the tune-out budget ```{=html}

Tune-Out Budget Calculator

words / min
words / min
```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: tune-out-02 listen_wpm <- 500 speak_wpm <- 150 briefing_minutes <- 12 spare_wpm <- listen_wpm - speak_wpm spare_words <- spare_wpm * briefing_minutes # Time the listener could "leave" if they mentally processed at listening speed: tune_out_seconds_per_min <- spare_wpm / listen_wpm * 60 par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) bp <- barplot(c(Speaking = speak_wpm, Listening = listen_wpm), col = c("#2980b9", "#16a085"), ylab = "Words per minute", main = "The gap the listener's mind fills") segments(bp[1], speak_wpm, bp[2], listen_wpm, lty = 2, lwd = 3, col = "#e74c3c") text(mean(bp), (speak_wpm + listen_wpm) / 2 + 20, labels = paste(spare_wpm, "spare"), cex = 1.3, col = "#e74c3c") cat(sprintf("Spare listening capacity: %d words/min\n", spare_wpm)) cat(sprintf("Spare words over the briefing %s\n", format(spare_words, big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("Tune-out time available %.0f seconds per minute\n", tune_out_seconds_per_min)) ```
Listening de-railers --- which one is Orion Tech's problem? - **Listening without focus** --- mind multitasking. - **Listening without respect (impatience)** --- deciding the other person is wrong and interrupting. - **Listening without respect (ego)** --- hearing only from your own perspective, not theirs. - **Listening with bias (defensive / adverse)** --- building your rebuttal while they talk, or listening only for points to attack. On Orion Tech it was mostly the first and last: dominant voices building responses instead of listening, quieter voices tuned out, and cross-cultural tone read through the listener's own filter rather than the speaker's intent.
## Choosing a communication method | | **Written** | **Verbal** | |---|---|---| | **Formal** | Complex problems, project plans, charters, long-distance --- *formal written* | Presentations and speeches --- *formal verbal* | | **Informal** | Memos, emails (careful: email is also a contract), texts, notes --- *informal written* | Meetings and conversations --- *informal verbal* | Should a PM try to control **all** communication between team members and outsiders? **Yes** --- and can they? **No.** The plan defines the important routes; it cannot police every hallway conversation. ## Performance reporting Different stakeholder questions need different reports: | Report | Answers | |---|---| | **Status** | Where does the project stand right now? | | **Progress** | What has been accomplished? | | **Trend** | Is performance improving or deteriorating over time? | | **Forecast** | What will status and performance be in the future? | | **Variance** | How do actual results compare to the plan? | | **Earned value** | Integrating scope, cost, and schedule into one performance picture (see [Chapter 12](12-Project-Control-Systems.qmd)). | Orion Tech's stakeholders were right to expect regular **status, progress, and forecast** reports --- they fund and approve the project, and reports give them transparency, accountability, and early warning. ## Key Takeaways - A **project** is temporary and unique; a **process** is permanent and repetitive. Only ~26 % of projects hit the full triple constraint --- which is why the discipline exists. - The **triple constraint** is scope--time--cost, enclosing **quality**. Move one side and another must move, or quality pays. - Five phases: **initiating, planning, executing, controlling, closing.** Planning decides the outcome; closing is the hardest to finish. - Decisions are weighed **safety → company → sponsor → customer → suppliers**; ethics rest on **responsibility, respect, fairness, honesty**. - ~**90 %** of a PM's time is communication. Build a written **communication plan** from stakeholder needs, and close every loop with **feedback**. - Channels grow as $n(n-1)/2$ --- faster than headcount. Plan routes; don't let everyone talk to everyone. - **Listening** is ~55 % of communication and the least trained; ~93 % of meaning is nonverbal. Watch for the **selective attention/interpretation/retention** filters and the de-railers. - Match the **method** (formal/informal × written/verbal) to the message, and the **report** (status/progress/trend/forecast/variance/EVM) to the stakeholder's question. ## Case Study: Meridian R/C — Week 2 ::: {.callout-tip .case-study title="📁 CASE STUDY FILE — Week 2: The Email That Didn't Reach Vancouver"} Three weeks after Daniel Cho green-lit the Meridian Trailblazer prototype, Sofia Reyes flagged a durability concern in the early drop-test data: the die-cast aluminium body and frame were flexing more than expected at the wheel-well corners. Priya Nandakumar's fix was straightforward --- thicken the aluminium wall from **1.2 mm to 1.5 mm**, a change that would not touch the tooling budget but would add a fraction of a gram per unit. You approved it the same afternoon and asked Marcus Webb to notify everyone downstream who depended on the old spec sheet. That is where it went wrong. Marcus fired off the update to the internal engineering distribution list --- Priya, Sofia, the CAD vendor, and you --- because that was the list he had bookmarked from the Week 1 kickoff. It was the right list for people *building* the part. It was not the right list for people *selling* it. Kestrel Retail Group's Category Buyer, **Renata Ford**, based out of **Vancouver**, had been working from the original 1.2 mm spec sheet to brief her own packaging and merchandising team on box dimensions and weight claims. Nobody had ever added her, or Kestrel's Vancouver office generally, to any distribution list --- because no such list existed. Renata found out about the change only when her packaging vendor's proof came back listing a spec that did not match Meridian's shipped sample. The fallout: a **3-day delay** while Kestrel's packaging vendor reprinted spec sheets and box art, and a **$4,000** rush-reprint charge nobody had budgeted for. Daniel Cho was patient about the money but blunt about the cause: *"This wasn't a design problem. It was a mailing-list problem."* You rebuilt the communication plan that week. A **weekly status email** now goes to a named, role-based distribution list --- not a bookmarked group of whoever was in the room at kickoff. A **biweekly steering call** with Daniel and Kestrel keeps the client in sync in real time instead of by forwarded email. And a **RACI matrix** now spells out, for every deliverable, who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed --- so "who else needs to know this" stops being a guess. The timing mattered too: the team was about to grow from 4 people to 7, taking the number of two-way communication channels from $n(n-1)/2 = 6$ to **21** --- more than triple the coordination load the new plan now had to carry. | Metric | Before the fix | After the fix | |---|---|---| | Distribution list | Ad hoc, engineering-only | Named, role-based (RACI-driven) | | Client sync | None scheduled | Weekly status email + biweekly steering call | | Team size | 4 | 7 | | Two-way channels ($n(n-1)/2$) | 6 | 21 | ::: ## Practice Problems
Problem 1: Channel count and a reorganization The RC-vehicle project currently routes all communication through a 6-person core team. A proposal would merge in 3 supplier engineers as full team members. (a) How many channels before and after? (b) By what percentage do channels increase versus the 50 % increase in headcount?
Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} before <- 6; after <- 9 ch <- function(n) n * (n - 1) / 2 cat("Before:", ch(before), "channels\n") cat("After :", ch(after), "channels\n") cat(sprintf("Headcount up %.0f%%, channels up %.0f%%\n", 100 * (after / before - 1), 100 * (ch(after) / ch(before) - 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Before: 15 channels After : 36 channels Headcount up 50%, channels up 140% ``` ::: ::: Headcount rises 50 %, channels rise 125 %. Merging them in as full members triples the coordination load of those three people; a defined liaison route would add far less.
Problem 2: Pick the method (automotive, food, defense) Choose formal/informal and written/verbal for each: 1. Notifying a defense customer that a delivered lot failed an acceptance test. 2. A daily 10-minute stand-up with the assembly team. 3. The project charter for the RC-vehicle launch. 4. Reminding a teammate that a drawing is due Friday.
Answers 1 --- **formal written** (contractual weight, complex, long-distance). 2 --- **informal verbal** (meeting). 3 --- **formal written** (plan/charter). 4 --- **informal written** (a text or short email; keep a light record).
Problem 3 (discussion): rebuild Orion Tech's communication system If you were the PM, redesign the tools, reporting, and meetings to prevent the failure.
Model answer Write a **communication plan before launch**. Use a mix: **email** for records, **Teams/Slack** for quick updates, **dashboards** for visual tracking, **video calls** for collaboration (so tone and context survive the offshore gap). Run **regular status meetings with an agenda and action items**, and have offshore developers present their own weekly updates so no group dominates. Send stakeholders a **weekly progress report** (status, cost, risk). Build **feedback loops**: every developer confirms, in their own words, what a requirement means before coding it. Use plain language, avoid idioms, and summarize decisions in writing.
